settings.title: The idea in under a minute
What happens when a customer asks?

items.title: The problem
items.text: Sam is a very good plumber, and his phone is quiet.

items.title: The question
items.text: A customer has a leak. She asks an engine, not Sam: who should I call?

items.title: How engines decide
items.text: Three questions. Can I read it? Do others confirm it? Do people choose it?

items.title: The fix
items.text: We raise all three: what the site says, what others confirm, what people pick.

items.title: The answer
items.text: Same question. Now every engine has a reason to name Sam.

settings.editor: Sam is a drawing, not a client. Read the equation in full

settings.title: Be the answer: how an engine decides who to name
settings.caption: Be the answer. Narrated, with captions. Written by Thomas D'Souza, Founder.
settings.fallback: Your browser does not play video. The five chapters beside it tell the same story.
settings.description: A narrated animated film: a customer asks an engine who to call, the engine asks three things (can I read it, do others confirm it, do people choose it), and raising all three changes the answer.
settings.transcript: This is Sam. He's the best plumber in town. But his phone is quiet. When a customer has a leak, she doesn't call Sam. She asks Google, Maps or ChatGPT: who should I call? Every engine decides the same way. It asks three things. Can I read what this business does? Do other sources confirm it? Do real people choose it? The three multiply. If one is zero, the answer is zero. So the engine names someone else. We fix all three. Read: Sam's site now says plainly what he does, where, and for whom. Confirm: listings, reviews and mentions that say the same thing. Choose: a listing people pick, and calls that prove it. Same question. Now every engine has a reason to name Sam. That is the D'Souza Equation. Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose. Be the answer.

settings.title: How does a search engine optimization company in the USA make you the answer?

settings.editor: With one equation that every engine obeys. Google, Maps, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity look different, but each does one job: take a person's question and name the most relevant business it can trust.
They differ in how they read. They agree on what they are looking for.

“Engines change. Your customer's question does not. Work on the question and every engine finds you.”

Thomas D'Souza, Founder, Relevant Search Media. In writing since 2025.

settings.title: Who is behind Relevant Search Media?

settings.editor: Thomas D'Souza is the founder of Relevant Search Media and the author of the D'Souza Equation, which explains how every search engine and AI assistant decides which business to name.

He has worked in digital marketing since 2010. Relevant Search Media, founded in 2020, has served more than 900 businesses from New Delhi, India, with a team of more than 100 specialists working US hours for clients across the United States.
Every page on this site carries his name, and every fact on it comes from one signed register. If something is wrong, the corrections page says how we fix it.

items.q: How many SEO agencies are there in the USA?
items.a:
Tens of thousands. Most keep their method private and show you a deck.

Relevant Search Media publishes its method as the D'Souza Standard, 413 numbered checks, so you can hold any agency, including us, to the same list. That is the difference to look for, not the count.

items.q: What is a search engine optimization company in the USA supposed to do?
items.a: Make your business the answer to the searches your customers make. In 2026 that means Google, Google Maps and the AI engines together. We map every search for your trade and city, run 413 checks, fix the biggest things first, and log each item with its link, so you can see the work every day.

items.q: Is there an affordable SEO company in the USA that still does real work?
items.a:
Affordable means the work is worth what it costs, and you can see it. Every plan is month to month, with no setup fee and no add-ons to buy.

Live work goes up by day 5, each item is logged with its link, and a report arrives every 15 days. Prices are discussed on the discovery call.

items.q: How soon will I see results?
items.a: Live work goes up on day 5 and your first report arrives on day 15. Rankings usually start moving between day 30 and day 60. By the end of month 4, at least half the customer searches in your map reach page one of Google, or we keep working at no charge until they do.

items.q: Can you get my business recommended by ChatGPT?
items.a: We do the work the AI engines use to choose a business: facts they can read, independent sources that confirm them, and signs that real people choose you. No one can honestly promise a placement in an AI answer, so we track where you are named, re-run the AI Recommendation Index every month, and report it.

items.q: Will you also work with my competitors?
items.a:
No. We take one business per trade per city.

Two roofers in the same city cannot both be the business an engine names, so your slot is yours for as long as you stay. The Open Board shows which trades and cities are taken.

items.q: Can I cancel, and what do I keep?
items.a:
Every plan is month to month. You cancel by email.

You keep everything: the website, the content, the listings and every account, from day one. Nothing is held back and nothing is charged to leave.

items.q: Is Relevant Search Media an SEO agency in the USA or in India?
items.a:
Both, honestly. The company is registered in New Delhi, India, and the whole team works US hours.

Every client is a US business, and every search we map is a US search. You get an SEO agency in the USA by market and by working day, at a cost structure that lets us keep every plan month to month.

settings.title: Common SEO issues: which one do you have?

settings.editor: Common SEO issues look alike from the inside, so go by what you see, not by what you were told. The table matches each symptom to the likely problem and to the first thing worth checking.
One business can have two of these at once. Fix them in the order shown, because being found comes before being chosen.

settings.text: See how the first fifteen days fix them

rows.b: Engines cannot read the business yet
rows.c: Search in a private window, on a phone, from inside your service area

settings.title: Why is my SEO not working?

settings.editor: When an owner asks “why is my SEO not working?”, the answer is nearly always one of three failed checks. Every engine takes a person’s question and names the most relevant business it can trust, and it decides with the same three checks.
Those checks are the D’Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose. That is why one fix works on Google, on Maps and in an AI answer.

settings.text: Read the equation in full

settings.title: Read fails: you cannot be found.
settings.text: The engine cannot tell plainly what the business is, where it works and what it answers. Nothing else counts until this passes.

settings.title: Confirm fails: AI names someone else.
settings.text: Your own site says it, but listings, reviews and mentions elsewhere do not say the same thing. The engine will not vouch for you.

settings.title: Choose fails: found, then passed over.
settings.text: People see you and then click, call or book someone else. Engines watch that choice and move the chosen business up.

settings.title: What should I check before I pay anyone to fix SEO problems?

settings.editor: Five checks, about ten minutes, no tools to buy. They tell you which problem you have, and they make any quote easier to judge.

settings.title: Search yourself
settings.text: Private window, your trade plus your city. Note whether you are on page one, on the map, or neither.

settings.title: Read your listing as a stranger
settings.text: Photos, hours, services, reviews and replies. Would you call this business?

settings.title: Ask an AI assistant
settings.text: Type the question a customer would ask. See which business it names, and why.

settings.title: Date the drop
settings.text: If calls fell, find the week it began. A date turns a mystery into a cause.

settings.editor: Your business is not showing up on Google because Google cannot yet read plainly what it is, where it works and what it answers, or cannot confirm that from anywhere else. The usual causes are an unverified or incomplete Business Profile, a website Google has not indexed, and details that differ from one listing to the next.

settings.text: Type the business name and city. If nothing of yours appears, Google has no confirmed record of the business.

items.q: Why is my business not on Google when I have a website?
items.a:
Having a website is not the same as being indexed. Google has to find the site, be allowed to read it and decide the pages are worth keeping.

Run the site: search above. If it returns nothing, the site is blocked, too new, or carries a noindex tag.

items.q: How to get my business on Google if it is brand new?
items.a:
Create a Google Business Profile and verify it, then publish a site that states plainly what you do and where. Add the business to the directories your trade uses, with the same name, address and phone.

A new business usually appears for its own name first, then for trade searches as reviews and mentions build.

items.q: Why did my business disappear from Google?
items.a: A business that was showing and then vanished usually has a suspended profile, a site change that blocked Google, or a drop after an update. Each leaves a date. Check the profile status first, then see our page on traffic that dropped.

A Business Profile costs nothing to create or verify, so a business not on Google is never there for lack of a fee.

Usually. AI assistants draw on the same sources search engines read: your site, your listings and what others say about you.

A business Google cannot read is rarely named by ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity. No one can promise an AI placement, so we track it monthly.

items.q: Can you guarantee my business shows up on Google?
items.a:
We commit in writing that at least half the customer searches in your map reach page one of Google by the end of month four, or we keep working at no charge.

We do not promise a position on Google Maps or in AI answers, because no one honestly can.

Win the choice on the results you already appear in. Complete the Business Profile, keep photos and reviews recent, and make the first screen of your page say what you do and where.

A bought lead is often sold to several businesses at once, and it stops the day you stop paying. A lead from search comes to you alone, from a person who chose you.

Read is your own site. Confirm is everyone else. Choose is what real customers did.

Start with what the assistant can read and check. Publish a plain facts page, complete your Google Business Profile, and get listed on the directories and review sites your trade uses.

A new business has few mentions, so consistency matters most: the same name, address, phone and services everywhere.

items.q: Does ChatGPT use Google rankings?
items.a:
Not directly. ChatGPT can search the web when a question needs current information, and it also draws on what many sources say about a business.

Ranking well makes it more likely your pages are among those it reads. It is not the same as being named in the answer.

items.q: Do I need an llms.txt file?
items.a:
It helps and costs little. An llms.txt file is a plain text page that tells AI systems what your site is and where its key pages are.

It is not a ranking switch, and not every assistant reads it. We publish one on this site, and you can read it at /llms.txt.

items.q: How often do AI answers change?
items.a:
Often. The same question can name different businesses on different days, and for different people. That is why one screenshot proves very little.

We put the same questions to the same assistants every month, so the trend is visible and one lucky answer is not mistaken for progress.

It is our public record of who ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity name for each trade in each city, re-run every month. The first run covers plumbing in the ten launch cities.

settings.title: Website traffic dropped suddenly: how to find the cause

settings.editor: When website traffic dropped suddenly, the first job is to find the week it began. A drop with a start date has a cause: a Google update, a change made to the site, a lost listing, or tracking that broke. Match the date to what changed that week and the cause is usually plain within ten minutes.
Date it first. Everything else follows from the date.

• 900+ businesses served

settings.title: Website traffic dropped suddenly: what do I check first?

settings.editor: Do these four checks in order. Each one narrows the cause, and none needs a paid tool.

settings.title: Date the drop
settings.text: In your analytics or call log, find the week the fall began. Write the date down.

settings.title: See what fell
settings.text: In Search Console, compare the weeks before and after. Is it every page, or a few? Search only, or all visits?

settings.title: Match Google’s updates
settings.text: Open Google’s Search Status Dashboard and look for a ranking update in that week.

settings.title: What should I do if I lost rankings after an update?

settings.editor: First, do not undo things in a panic. Google says a page that falls after a core update has not necessarily done anything wrong, and that there may be nothing specific to fix.

What helps is honest comparison. Open the pages that rose for your searches and ask what they answer that yours does not. Improvements are often recognised over the following weeks and at later updates.

settings.title: How long does it take to recover lost traffic?

settings.editor: That turns on the cause. A block or a missing redirect is a one-day repair, and the pages come back as Google recrawls them over days or weeks.
A fall after an update is slower and nobody can promise its return. On our plans the first fixes go live by day 5 and the first report arrives on day 15.

settings.title: What do owners ask when traffic falls?

settings.editor: The five questions owners ask most once the numbers fall. Something else on your mind? Try the Ask page.

items.q: Why has my website traffic dropped overnight?
items.a:
An overnight fall across the whole site is usually technical: a noindex tag left on after a rebuild, a robots block, an expired certificate or a host problem.

If only search visits fell and the site works, look for a Google update or a change to your Business Profile on that date.

items.q: I lost rankings after an update. Will they come back?
items.a:
Sometimes, and nobody can promise it. Google re-weighs what it values at each update, so pages can return when they improve or when the next update lands.

If you lost rankings after an update, compare your pages with the ones that rose and close the gap.

items.q: Can a website redesign cause a traffic drop?
items.a:
Yes, and it is one of the most common causes. A redesign often changes page addresses, removes text Google relied on, or goes live with a noindex tag still in place.

Keep the old addresses or redirect each one, and check indexing the day the new site launches.

items.q: How do I know if Google penalised my site?
items.a:
Open Search Console and look at the Manual actions report. If Google has taken action, it says so there and names the reason.

Most falls are not penalties. They are updates, technical mistakes or stronger rivals, and each is handled differently.

items.q: Should I pay for ads until my traffic recovers?
items.a:
Ads can replace lost calls while the cause is fixed, and for some businesses that is the right bridge. They do not repair what caused the fall.

Find and fix the cause first, or the ads become a permanent cost for a problem that had a cure.

pages.title: The D'Souza Equation: How Search Engines Rank Websites

seo.title: The D'Souza Equation: How Search Engines Rank Websites
seo.description: The D'Souza Equation explains how search engines rank websites and how AI picks a business. Relevance equals Read times Confirm times Choose.

settings.editor: Home › The Equation

settings.title: The D'Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose

settings.editor: The D'Souza Equation says Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose. A search engine or an AI assistant names a business when it can read plainly what the business is, when independent sources confirm it, and when real people choose it. The three are multiplied, so a business that fails one check is not named.
One equation. Every engine obeys it.

settings.text: Book a discovery call
Ask a question

settings.editor: 20 to 30 minutes with Thomas. No audit to buy first.

• 900+ businesses served
  • 100+ specialists on US hours
  • In digital marketing since 2010

It is a way of seeing what every engine has to decide before it names a business. Google, Maps, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity look different, but each takes a person’s question and names the most relevant business it can trust.
Move the three dials below. The lights are customers asking, and the number is how many of every hundred are sent to you.

settings.plain: Out of 100 people who ask, the engine sends roughly {n} your way. Let one check fall to nothing and it sends none.

terms.name: Read
terms.q: Is it plain from the site itself who this is and which questions it settles?
terms.where: clear facts, direct answers, clean structure and markup on your own pages.

terms.name: Confirm
terms.q: Does the rest of the web describe the business the same way?
terms.where: matching listings, real reviews, mentions and press on other sites.

terms.name: Choose
terms.q: When shown this business, do searchers pick it?
terms.where: a listing and a first screen that win the click, the call and the return visit.

settings.editor: For example, when a customer asks “who fixes a burst pipe?”, the engine reads each plumber’s site, checks what others say, and looks at who people chose. With Read at 80, Confirm at 70 and Choose at 75, about 42 in 100 are sent to you.

settings.text: See the five problems the equation explains

settings.title: How do search engines rank websites?

settings.editor: How do search engines rank websites, and how do AI assistants pick one business to name? With three checks. Each check is a question the engine asks, and each has a place where the work is done.

settings.title: Read
settings.text: The engine has to understand the business from its own pages: who it is, what it does, where, and which questions it settles.

settings.title: Confirm
settings.text: The engine then looks elsewhere. If directories, review sites and other publishers describe the business the same way, it trusts what it read.

settings.title: Choose
settings.text: Last, the engine watches behaviour. A business that searchers click, call and come back to is shown to the next searcher.

settings.title: Why is the relevance equation a multiplication?

items.q: How does Google rank websites, and is this its formula?

settings.title: Facts.

settings.text: Structured data that labels the facts for a machine: the organisation, the place, the questions, the author.

settings.title: Do AI assistants read a site differently from Google?

settings.editor: They fetch pages with their own crawlers, such as GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot, and many sites block them without knowing. A robots.txt file can welcome each by name.
They also favour text that answers directly. A paragraph that states a fact in full is quoted; one that hints at it is skipped. An llms.txt file helps by listing the key pages in plain text.

items.q: How do I know if Google has indexed my site?
items.a:
Search site: followed by your domain. The results are the pages Google holds. Search Console shows the same thing in more detail, with the reason for each page it left out.

If the count is far below the pages you published, something on this page’s list of blockers applies.

items.q: Does my site need to be fast to be read?
items.a:
It needs to respond. A server that times out or returns errors is read less often and less deeply. Speed beyond that mostly affects whether people stay.

The Standard has 24 checks on speed and stability for that reason.

items.q: Is a website builder a problem?
items.a:
Not by itself. Most builders produce pages an engine can read. Trouble comes from settings: a noindex switch left on, text drawn by script, or addresses that change at each edit.

Run the four checks above; they work on any platform.

items.q: What is structured data, in plain words?
items.a:
It is a label attached to a fact. It tells a machine that this string is a phone number, that one is an opening hour, and this block is a question with its answer.

It does not replace clear writing. It makes clear writing unmistakable.

items.q: How long until a fixed page is read again?
items.a:
Google says crawling can take from a few days to a few weeks. Asking for a recrawl in Search Console usually shortens it for an important page.

items.q: What is the difference between a citation and a backlink?
items.a:
A citation is a listing of the business name, address and phone on another site, such as a directory. A backlink is a link from another site to yours.

Both confirm the business. Citations prove the place; links and mentions prove that others find it worth pointing to.

items.q: How many directory listings do I need?
items.a:
There is no number to hit. Start with the listings your customers and your trade actually use, and make each one identical to your Google profile.

Accuracy across a dozen good listings beats volume across hundreds nobody reads.

items.q: Can I pay for reviews or links?
items.a:
You can, and you should not. Paid reviews break the platforms’ rules and the law in many places, and bought links are what search engines discount first.

Confirmation only works because it comes from someone with no reason to flatter you.

items.q: Does social media count as a trust signal?
items.a:
It counts as evidence that the business is real and active. A profile with the same name, address and services, posting now and then, supports the rest.

It is not a ranking lever by itself, and an abandoned profile helps less than none.

items.q: How long does confirmation take to build?
items.a:
Fixing mismatched listings is quick and shows within weeks. Earning reviews and mentions is steady work, month after month.

items.q: Does Google really use clicks to rank pages?
items.a:
Google has said for years that it studies how people interact with results, and court filings have described systems that learn from it. The details are not public.

You do not need them. A result people prefer is a result an engine has every reason to keep showing.

items.q: What is a good click-through rate?
items.a:
It depends on the position and the search, so a single target is misleading. Compare a page with itself over time, and with the pages ranked around it.

A title and description that answer the search directly lift the rate at any position.

items.q: Why do I rank well and still get few calls?
items.a:
Because ranking gets you seen and something after that loses the choice: the listing, the first screen, or a phone nobody answers.

Run the four checks on this page. The moment you lose people at is usually obvious once you look.

items.q: Do reviews belong to Confirm or to Choose?
items.a:
Both. To an engine, reviews on independent platforms confirm that the business is real. To a searcher, the same reviews decide the choice.

That double duty is why asking every customer, and replying to each review, repays the effort twice.

items.q: Can design alone raise how often I am chosen?
items.a:
It helps when it removes friction: a clear first screen, a visible number, a short form. It does not help when it only decorates.

People choose on clarity and proof. Design serves both, or it is in the way.

settings.title: How is a page scored against the checklist?

settings.editor: Each check ends one of three ways: pass, fail, or not testable yet. A page is published only with no failed check.

Not testable yet is used honestly. Some checks need Search Console data, a second reviewer’s signature or seven days to pass, and they are listed as open until that exists. They are never counted as passes.

settings.title: Pass.
settings.text: The page was measured and met the check. The measurement is recorded with the date.

settings.title: Fail.
settings.text: The page did not meet it. It is fixed and measured again before anything is published.

settings.title: Not testable yet.
settings.text: The check needs data or a person that the page alone cannot supply. It stays open, by name.

settings.title: Can I run this website SEO audit on my own site?

settings.editor: Yes. Nothing here is behind a form. An owner can work through the groups that apply to one page in an afternoon, and the checks say plainly what to look for.
Where it gets heavy is scale: 413 checks across every page, every listing and every AI answer, repeated as engines change. That is the work a team does.

settings.text: What to check first, by problem

settings.title: Pick one page
settings.text: Start with the page that should bring the most customers, usually the home page or a main service.

settings.title: Open the page groups
settings.text: Titles and descriptions, headings and copy, images and conversion elements all apply to a single page.

settings.title: Mark each line
settings.text: Pass, fail or cannot tell. Be strict: a check you are unsure of is a fail until shown otherwise.

settings.title: Fix the fails in order
settings.text: Work from the top of the list. The early groups decide whether the later ones matter.

settings.title: How often does the Standard change?

settings.editor: It is versioned and dated. This is version 1.0 of 23 Nov 2026. When a new engine or a new kind of question matters, checks are added as numbered rows and the version moves.
A check is never quietly reworded. Changes are recorded on the corrections page.

items.q: Why publish the whole checklist?
items.a:
Because a method you cannot see cannot be checked. Publishing all 413 lines lets a client hold us to them, and lets anyone compare another agency’s work with the same list.

It also means we cannot quietly skip the hard ones.

items.q: Do all 413 checks apply to every page?
items.a:
No. 193 apply to every page, 149 to the site as a whole and 71 to things beyond the site, such as listings, reviews and profiles.

A single page is held to the page checks; the site and off-site checks are run once and re-run on a schedule.

items.q: What does “not testable yet” mean?
items.a:
It means the answer is not in the page. A check that needs real-visitor speed data, a second reviewer’s sign-off or a week of indexing cannot be judged at publish time.

Those checks stay open and are closed, by name, when the data arrives.

items.q: How is this different from a one-off SEO audit?
items.a:
A one-off audit is one run of a list on one day. The Standard is the list itself, run on day three and then kept running.

An audit that is never acted on changes nothing, which is why our plans ship fixes from day 5.

settings.title: What is the SEO strategy meaning behind the method?

settings.editor: An SEO strategy, in its plain meaning, is a decision about which searches to win and in what order to do the work. Ours follows the D’Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose.
So the order is fixed. First an engine has to read you, then others have to confirm you, then people have to choose you. The weakest of the three is raised first.

settings.title: Read
settings.text: Make every engine able to read what the business is, what it does and where.

settings.title: Confirm
settings.text: Make listings, reviews and mentions elsewhere say the same thing.

settings.title: Choose
settings.text: Make the listing and the first screen win the click and the call.

items.q: What is SEO strategy?
items.a:
It is the plan for being the business an engine names: which customer searches to win, what to fix first and how the work is checked. A list of tasks is not a strategy.

Ours is written down as the D’Souza Method, and every client gets the same order of work.

items.q: What is SEO strategy in digital marketing?
items.a:
In digital marketing, SEO strategy is the part that earns attention instead of renting it. Ads stop when the budget stops; a page that answers a search keeps being found.

It sits beside ads, social and email, and usually feeds all three with the questions customers actually ask.

items.q: What is SEO strategy for business owners who are short of time?
items.a:
One that asks little of you. Ours needs one conversation on day 1, a look at the plan on day 4 and a few minutes every 15 days to mark which leads were relevant.

Everything else is done by the team and logged where you can see it.

items.q: How to create SEO strategy for your business?
items.a:
Start with the searches. List what your customers type, group them by what they want, and check which of them an engine can already read, confirm and see chosen.

Then fix the weakest part first. The 413 checks of the D’Souza Standard are published if you want to do it yourself.

items.q: How to build SEO strategy that still works when Google changes?
items.a:
Build it on the customer’s question, not on the engine’s habits. Engines change how they read; they do not change what they are looking for.

A business that is readable, confirmed elsewhere and chosen by real people holds its place through updates.

settings.title: What is D'Souza's Law of Search?

settings.editor: It rests on two observations. Put together, they explain why a business that chases each new engine falls behind, and why one that answers its customers keeps its place.

settings.text: The equation that follows from it

settings.title: Every engine is a relevance machine.
settings.text: Google, Maps, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, YouTube and the social networks look different. Each does one job: it takes a person’s question and chooses the most relevant answer it can trust.

items.q: Why is SEO not dead?
items.a:
Because people still ask questions, and something still has to choose an answer. That choice is what SEO has always worked on.

The engines doing the choosing have multiplied. The need to be the business they can read, confirm and see chosen has not gone anywhere.

items.q: Is SEO dead because of AI?
items.a:
No. AI assistants read the web, weigh what independent sources say and learn from what people choose. Those are the three things search work has always built.

What AI has ended is the shortcut. Thin pages written for a ranking do not get quoted in an answer.

items.q: Is SEO dead in 2026?
items.a:
In 2026 it is busier than ever, and split across more engines. A customer may ask Google in the morning, a map at lunch and an assistant in the evening.

The work that survives is the work aimed at the question, because the question is the only part common to all three.

items.q: Is SEO dead or evolving in 2026?
items.a:
Evolving, in one direction: from ranking a page to being named as the answer. The reading has become stricter and the room at the top smaller.

A method built on the customer’s question absorbs each new engine as one more reader, without starting again.

items.q: Do I need a different service for every AI engine?
items.a:
No. Each new engine produced a new label, and under each label the job is the same: be readable, be confirmed, be chosen.

We sell one body of work and check it against every engine in our register.

settings.title: SEO vs GEO vs AEO vs AIO, and where each fits

settings.editor: SEO vs GEO comes down to which engine is being served: SEO is the work of being found in search results, and GEO, generative engine optimization, is being named in an AI assistant’s answer. settings.title: How does Google search work now, and how does AI answer

settings.editor: How does Google search work? In three stages that Google itself names: it crawls the web to find pages, indexes what it understands of them, and serves the results it judges most useful for each search. What has changed is the last stage: more and more often an AI now reads those results and writes the answer for the person.
Same three stages. A new reader at the end.

settings.title: How does Google search work, step by step?

settings.editor: Google describes its own search in three stages. A page has to get through all three before anyone can find it, and each stage is a place where a business can be lost.

settings.text: On page SEO: can every engine read you?

settings.caption: The three stages of Google search and what goes wrong at each

rows.b: Programs called crawlers follow links and fetch pages
rows.c: The page is blocked, unlinked or too slow to fetch

rows.b: Google works out what each page is about and stores it
rows.c: The words are missing from the page, or the page duplicates another

rows.b: For each search it ranks the stored pages and shows the most useful
rows.c: Nothing confirms the business, or people pick someone else

settings.editor: How do AI Overviews work? Google’s Gemini models read pages from Google’s own index and write a short summary above the results, with links to the pages they drew on. AI Mode does the same in a longer, conversational form.
They do not replace the three stages. They sit on top of them, so a page that was never crawled or indexed cannot be quoted in the summary.

settings.text: AI Overview optimization

settings.editor: How does ChatGPT search work? When a question needs current information, ChatGPT searches the web, reads a handful of pages and writes an answer that cites them. It also has its own crawler, OAI-SearchBot, which sites can allow or block by name.
Other assistants follow the same pattern with different sources. The reading is new; the need to be readable, confirmed and chosen is not.

settings.text: How to get my business recommended by ChatGPT

settings.title: What do all of these have in common?

settings.editor: Each of them takes a person’s question and names the most relevant answer it can trust. That is the first observation behind the D’Souza Equation: Relevance = Read × Confirm × Choose.
Crawling and indexing are Read. Agreement from other sources is Confirm. What people click, call and return to is Choose.

settings.title: Read
settings.text: Crawling and indexing: can the engine fetch the page and understand it?

settings.title: Confirm
settings.text: Serving: do other sources say the same thing about the business?

settings.title: Choose
settings.text: Serving: when shown the business, do people pick it?

settings.title: How do I check where my site stops?

settings.editor: Three checks, one for each stage, in about ten minutes. They show which stage your business is stuck at.

settings.title: Crawling
settings.text: Open yoursite.com/robots.txt. A line reading “Disallow: /” shuts every crawler out.

settings.title: Indexing
settings.text: Search site: followed by your domain. Compare the count with the pages you published.

settings.title: Serving
settings.text: Search your trade and city in a private window. See whether you are on the map, in the AI answer, or on page one.

settings.editor: For example, an HVAC company in Dallas might pass steps 1 and 2 and still be missing at step 3 for “ac repair dallas”. Then the site is read, and the problem is confirmation or choice.

items.q: How Google search works, in one sentence?
items.a:
It finds pages, works out what each one is about, and for every search shows the pages it judges most useful to that person, in that place, at that moment.

Everything else, from links to reviews to AI summaries, is detail inside those three steps.

items.q: How does Google search work so fast?
items.a:
Because the hard work is done before you search. Google has already crawled and indexed the pages, so a search is a lookup in a prepared index, not a fresh read of the web.

That is also why a new page cannot appear until Google has crawled it.

items.q: How does the Google search engine work for a local search?
items.a:
For a local search Google adds place to the picture. It says local results turn mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and it draws on Business Profiles as well as websites.

That is why a complete, accurate profile matters as much as the site.

items.q: Does Google search work the same for everyone?
items.a:
No. Results change with where you are, what you searched before and the device in your hand. Two people can type the same words and see different businesses.

A private window, on a phone, inside your service area gives the fairest test.

items.q: Does an AI answer use the same pages as search?
items.a:
Largely, yes. Google’s AI answers are written from pages in Google’s index, and assistants such as ChatGPT search the web and cite what they read.

A page that search engines cannot read is not available to quote in an AI answer either.

settings.title: How do I check the SEO factors on my own site?

settings.editor: Start with four elements that most often hold a small business back. Each takes a couple of minutes.

settings.title: Title tag
settings.text: Open your home page and read the browser tab. It should say what you do and where, in under 60 characters.

settings.title: Google Business Profile category
settings.text: Open your profile. The primary category should be your main trade, not a broader one.

settings.title: NAP consistency
settings.text: Compare your name, address and phone on three listings. They should match to the letter.

settings.title: Call to action
settings.text: On a phone, can a visitor call or book from the first screen with one tap?

settings.editor: For example, a plumber in Miami whose title tag reads “Home” has left the most-read element on the page empty. It is one of 113, and one of the quickest to put right.

items.q: What are SEO ranking factors?
items.a:
They are the signals an engine uses to decide which page or business answers a search most usefully: what the page says, how the site is built, what others say about it and how people respond.

We group them as Read, Confirm and Choose, the three terms of the D’Souza Equation.

items.q: What is Google ranking factors, and does Google publish them?
items.a:
Google publishes guidance and names some systems, but not a complete, weighted list. Anyone claiming to hold the full list is guessing.

What can be known is what an engine needs: to read you, to confirm you, and to see you chosen. That is what our elements cover.

items.q: How many SEO ranking factors are there?
items.a:
Nobody outside the engines knows, and the number changes. The often-quoted figure of 200 was never an official list.

We count what can be worked on. That comes to 113 elements, tested by the 413 checks of the D’Souza Standard.

items.q: What are local SEO ranking factors?
items.a:
Google says local results turn mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. In practice that means the Business Profile, its category and services, reviews, and listings that agree with each other.

Sixteen of our elements sit under listings, and most local work happens there.

items.q: What is SEO ranking, and how is it different from being named?
items.a:
A ranking is a position in a list of results. Being named is an engine choosing your business as its answer, on a map, in a box or in an assistant’s reply.

Rankings still matter. Being named is what the newer engines do instead.

items.q: What are local SEO services?
items.a:
They are the work that gets a business shown to people nearby: on the map, in local results and in answers about the area. The Google Business Profile, reviews and matching listings do most of it.

A website helps, and a local business can be found without a large one.

items.q: How does local SEO work?
items.a:
Google says it ranks local results mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. Relevance is how well the profile matches the search, distance is how near you are, and prominence is how well known.

You cannot move your address. You can raise the other two.

items.q: Is local SEO different from regular SEO?
items.a:
It is the same equation with different evidence. Regular search leans on pages and links; local search leans on the listing, reviews and directories.

A business that serves a city needs both, and the work overlaps more than the two names suggest.

items.q: Do I need a street address to appear on the map?
items.a:
No. Google lets a business that travels to its customers hide its address and show a service area instead. Plumbers, cleaners and many contractors are set up this way.

The profile still has to be verified, complete and consistent with your other listings.

items.q: How long does local SEO take to show?
items.a:
Corrections to a profile and to mismatched listings often show within weeks. Reviews and prominence build month by month.

On our plans the first fixes go live by day 5, and the first report arrives on day 15.

items.q: Does Google offer SEO services itself?

Paid placement on Google is advertising, and it is labelled as sponsored.

items.q: Can you guarantee an assistant will name my business?

items.q: How is AI SEO measured?

By asking. The same customer questions are put to the same assistants every month, and the answers are recorded: who was named, and what was said.

One lucky answer proves nothing. A trend over months does.

items.q: What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?
items.a:
It is making your page the source an engine quotes when it gives one answer instead of a list. That covers answer boxes, related-question lists and voice replies.

The method is plain: ask the question in the heading, answer it at once, and mark it up.

items.q: How does answer engine optimization work?
items.a:
An engine looks for a passage that answers the question completely and briefly, from a page it trusts. A direct answer of a few sentences under a matching heading is easy to lift.

Background, history and sales talk before the answer make the passage unusable.

items.q: How do I do answer engine optimization on my own site?
items.a:
Take your most asked question, make it the heading, and write the answer in 40 to 60 words straight under it. Then add the next questions a customer would ask.

Keep every fact true and checkable. An engine that catches one wrong answer trusts the page less.

items.q: Is AEO different from generative engine optimization?
items.a:
They overlap. AEO is about being quoted as the single answer; generative engine optimization is about being named or cited when an assistant writes a longer reply.

Both need readable facts. GEO leans more on what other sources say about you.

items.q: Do answer boxes take clicks away from my site?
items.a:
Sometimes a person reads the answer and stops. But the business quoted is the one they remember and call, and a voice assistant gives only one name.

Being the quoted source is worth more than being the second link under someone else’s answer.

items.q: What is technical SEO in simple words?
items.a:
It is making sure a search engine can open your pages, understand them and keep them. Nothing in it changes what you say to customers.

Think of it as the wiring. Nobody sees it, and nothing works without it.

items.q: How important is technical SEO?
items.a:
It decides whether the rest of the work can count. A fine page that is blocked, slow or duplicated may never be shown.

It is not the whole job. A readable site still has to be confirmed and chosen.

items.q: What is the difference between technical SEO and on-page SEO?
items.a:
On-page work is about what a page says: its title, headings and answers. The technical side is about whether engines can reach and process that page.

Both sit in Read. One is the words, the other is the delivery.

items.q: How to fix technical SEO issues?
items.a:
Start with whatever stops reading: blocked pages, broken redirects, missing canonical tags. Then deal with speed, then markup.

Fix one class of fault at a time and re-test, so you know which change did what.

items.q: What do schema markup services cover?
items.a:
Writing the structured data that labels a page for machines: the business, its services, its questions and answers, its articles.

The markup must match what a visitor can see. Markup that claims more than the page shows is ignored or penalised.

items.q: What is link building?
items.a:
It is the work of earning links from other websites to yours. Search engines treat a link from a relevant, independent site as a sign that your business is real and worth noting.

The word “building” misleads. Good links are earned, not manufactured.

items.q: Is link building still relevant to SEO?
items.a:
Yes. Links remain one of the ways Google judges a site, though they count for less than they once did, and quality counts far more than number.

Mentions matter to AI assistants too, which lean on what independent sources say about a business.

items.q: Can I buy links safely?
items.a:
No. Google’s spam policies treat bought links that pass ranking credit as link spam. A site caught can be demoted or removed from results.

Paid placements are allowed when they are marked as sponsored. They then pass no ranking credit.

items.q: How many links do I need?
items.a:
There is no number. What matters is how your mentions compare with the businesses shown above you for the same search.

For a local trade, a dozen relevant local and trade mentions can outweigh hundreds of unrelated ones.

items.q: What about bad links pointing at my site?
items.a:
Most can be ignored. Google says its systems discount spam links by themselves in nearly all cases.

The disavow tool exists for sites with a manual action, or with a history of bought links. Used carelessly it does harm.

items.q: What are social media marketing services?
items.a:
They are the work of running a business’s presence on social networks: setting up profiles, planning and publishing posts, answering comments and reporting results.

items.q: What is social media management, compared with marketing?

Management is the daily running of the accounts: posting, replying, keeping details correct. Marketing is the plan behind it, meaning who you want to reach and why.

items.q: Which networks should my business be on?

Often enough that the newest post is always recent, and no more often than you can sustain. For many local businesses that is two or three times a week.

A steady rhythm matters more than volume. Gaps of months do the damage.

items.q: What is ecommerce SEO?
items.a:
It is search work for an online store. The aim is for category and product pages to appear when someone searches for what you sell.

It differs from ordinary site work mainly in scale. A store has many similar pages, and keeping them distinct is half the job.

items.q: How to do ecommerce SEO on a new store?
items.a:
Start with categories. Decide what search each one answers, and write a short, useful introduction for it.

Then write your own product descriptions, add product markup and connect Google Merchant Center. Leave blog posts until all of those are done and working.

items.q: How to improve ecommerce SEO on an existing store?
items.a:
Find out what Google has indexed and remove the waste first: filtered duplicates, empty categories, old test pages.

Then improve the categories that already get impressions in Search Console. They are the nearest to earning sales, so work on them pays back soonest.

items.q: Do product reviews matter for search?
items.a:
Yes. Reviews add fresh, honest text to a product page, and star ratings can appear in results when marked up correctly.

They must be real reviews from real buyers. Google’s rules do not allow ratings a store wrote for itself.

items.q: Can AI assistants recommend products from my store?
items.a:
They can. Assistants draw on product pages, feeds and reviews when someone asks what to buy.

Clear product details, accurate markup and independent reviews make a store easier to cite. No one can promise a recommendation, and we do not.

items.q: What is B2B SEO?
items.a:
It is search work for a company whose customers are other companies. The searches are fewer and more specific, and each enquiry is worth more.

The aim is not traffic. It is to be present each time a serious buyer looks something up.

items.q: How is it different from consumer SEO?
items.a:
A consumer may search once and buy. A business buyer searches many times, involves colleagues and compares suppliers before speaking to anyone.

So the site needs pages for every stage, and the measure is qualified enquiries, not visits.

items.q: How long does B2B search work take to pay back?
items.a:
Longer than consumer work, because the sale itself is slow. Pages can rank within months; the deals they start may close a quarter or two later.

We report every 15 days on rankings and enquiries, so progress is visible well before revenue.

items.q: Should we publish prices?
items.a:
That is your decision. Buyers do search for pricing, and a page that explains how your pricing works can rank for it without listing figures.

What matters is that the page answers honestly, so a buyer is not left guessing.

items.q: Would a B2B SEO agency tell us to start a blog?
items.a:
A careful one would not, for its own sake. You need a page for each real buyer question, and some of those suit an article.

A blog filled to a schedule, with no search behind each post, mostly adds pages nobody finds.

items.q: What does digital marketing include?
items.a:
Search, AI answers, business listings, social media, reviews, email, paid advertising and the website that ties them together.

Our own work covers search, AI answers, the Google profile, social media, content, links, reviews and the website. Those are the channels a customer meets without an advert.

items.q: What is a digital marketing company?
items.a:
A firm that plans and carries out a business’s online marketing. Some specialise in one channel; others, like us, run several as one programme.

The test is whether the channels are planned together or simply billed together. Ask to see the plan before you sign anything.

items.q: What are internet marketing services?
items.a:
Another name for the same thing. Internet marketing, online marketing and digital marketing are used interchangeably.

The older terms are still searched often, which is why you will see all three on agency sites. The work behind each name is identical.

items.q: Are digital marketing services for small business worth it?
items.a:
They are when they bring enquiries you would not otherwise have had. For a local business, search and the Google profile usually pay back first.

Start with the channel your customers already use to look for you, and measure enquiries, not followers.

items.q: What is an AI digital marketing agency?
items.a:
The phrase is used two ways: an agency that uses AI tools in its work, or one that works on being recommended by AI assistants.

We mean the second. Being named by ChatGPT or Gemini is now part of being found.

items.q: What are web design services?
items.a:
They cover planning and designing a website: which pages it has, how each is laid out, what it says and how it looks on different screens.

Building the site is web development. Many firms, ours included, do both as one job.

items.q: What is the difference between web design and web development?
items.a:
Design decides what the site contains and how it looks and reads. Development turns that into working pages on a server.

The two cannot be separated cleanly. A design that ignores how it will be built is usually slow.

items.q: Should I redesign or repair my current site?
items.a:
Repair it if the structure is sound and the faults are specific: slow pages, a broken form, thin text. Redesign if the pages do not match what customers search.

An audit answers the question in a day. It is cheaper than guessing.

items.q: Will a new design hurt my rankings?
items.a:
It can, if addresses change without redirects or if pages that rank are dropped. Both are avoidable.

Before any redesign we list every page that earns visits and make sure each one survives or is redirected.

items.q: How long does a new website take?
items.a:
It depends on the number of pages and how quickly words and photos are agreed. The writing usually takes longer than the drawing.

We give a timetable once the site map is settled, because that is when the size of the job is known.

items.q: Do web developers design websites?
items.a:
Some do, but they are different skills. A developer writes the code that makes a site work. A designer decides what it contains and how it looks.

On a small project one team often does both. It helps when design and build are planned together.

items.q: Which platform should my site be built on?
items.a:
The one you can edit yourself and that a future developer can take over. For most small businesses that is a widely used content system.

A rare or proprietary platform ties you to whoever built it. Ask what happens if you leave.

items.q: Will a site builder do the job?
items.a:
For a simple site, often yes. Hosted builders have improved, and a clear five-page site can rank from one.

They struggle with speed and control as a site grows. The checks on this page show whether yours is holding up.

items.q: What happens to my rankings at launch?
items.a:
They should hold if every address is redirected and the content that ranked is kept. Some movement for a few weeks is normal.

We confirm indexing after launch and watch the pages that earned visits before, so a drop is caught and traced quickly.

items.q: Who owns the site when it is finished?
items.a:
You do. The code, the content, the domain and the hosting account are all in your name or transferred to you.

If you later move to another provider, nothing needs our permission. That is part of our month-to-month terms: the client owns everything created.

items.q: What are application development services?
items.a:
They are the planning, design, building and upkeep of software applications. The term covers mobile apps, web apps that run in a browser, and internal tools for staff.

A good provider handles all four stages, so the people who built the product also maintain it.

items.q: Web app or mobile app: which do I need?
items.a:
A web app runs in the browser and needs no installation. A mobile app is installed from a store and can use the phone’s camera, location and notifications more fully.

If the task does not need those, a web app is usually quicker and cheaper to build.

items.q: What should I ask a mobile app development company?
items.a:
Ask who will own the code and the store accounts, how often you will see a working version, and what maintenance costs after launch.

Also ask a mobile app development company whether you need an app at all. An honest one will sometimes say no.

items.q: How long does an app take to build?
items.a:
A simple app with a handful of screens can take a few months. More screens, payments or links to other systems add time.

The timetable is fixed once the screens are agreed, because that is when the size of the work is known.

items.q: Can people find my app through search?
items.a:
Partly. Store listings are searched inside the App Store and Google Play, and Google can show an app’s public web page.

What sits inside is mostly invisible to search engines, so the product needs a proper page on your website.

items.q: What is custom CRM development?
items.a:
It is building a customer relationship system for one business, around its own steps and words, in place of adapting a general product.

The result does less than a large commercial CRM, on purpose. It does what your team needs and nothing they will ignore.

items.q: What is a CRM, in plain terms?
items.a:
CRM stands for customer relationship management. In practice it is a shared list of every enquiry and customer, with what was said and what happens next.

Its job is simple: nobody who contacted you is forgotten, and anyone on the team can pick up the thread.

items.q: How long does it take to build a CRM?
items.a:
A focused system for a small team can be in use within a couple of months. Links to accounting, phones or scheduling add time.

Most of the early effort goes into agreeing the process. The build is quicker once that is settled.

items.q: Should I just use an existing product?
items.a:
Often, yes. If a well-known CRM fits your process with light set-up, it is the sensible choice, and we will say so.

A custom CRM earns its place when staff are working around the tool more than with it.

items.q: Can it show which marketing brings customers?
items.a:
Yes, and that is one of the main reasons to have one. Each enquiry carries its source, so you can see which page or search led to paid work.

That turns marketing reports from visits and rankings into customers and revenue.

items.q: What do logo design services include?
items.a:
A set of logo options to choose from, refinement of the one you pick, and final files in the formats printers and websites need.

Good logo design services also show the mark in use: on a card, a sign and a phone screen, not only on a white page.

items.q: What is the difference between a logo and a brand?
items.a:
A logo is one mark. A brand is the whole impression: the name, the look, the way you write and how customers describe you.

Design can supply the look. The rest is earned through the work you do for customers.

items.q: Do I own the logo when it is done?
items.a:
You should, and with us you do. You receive the original editable files and the right to use and change them as you wish.

Always confirm this in writing with any designer. Some keep the originals and charge for each new use.

items.q: Does design affect search?
items.a:
Indirectly. A consistent name and logo across your site and profiles helps engines treat them as one business.

Images also affect speed. Graphics prepared at the right size and in the right format keep pages fast, which Google measures on every visit.

items.q: Can you work with the logo I already have?
items.a:
Yes. Often the mark is sound and only its use has drifted. We tidy the files, fix the colours and build the kit around it.

A full redesign is worth it only when the existing mark cannot be read small or no longer fits the business.
